newsitem.title: CHINA: China says more U.S. Congress visits to boost ties.
newsitem.headline: China says more U.S. Congress visits to boost ties.

text.p: China said on Tuesday that more visits to China by U.S. congressmen would help to further boost the improvement in relations between Beijing and Washington.

A record 35 representatives and senators visited China in January -- compared with 39 for all of 1996 -- and the delegations marked a new atmosphere in Sino-U.S. ties, the official Xinhua news agency said.

"More visits to China by the U.S. Congress will help increase mutual understanding and trust," it said. "Each of these congressional delegations had a courteous reception and each was viewed with importance by Chinese leaders."
Analysts say Beijing is slowly realising the importance of wooing U.S. lawmakers, many of whom have long been critical of China's foreign policy and human rights record.
China's charm offensive has been led by leaders such as President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng, who have made a point of meeting the visiting congressmen.

The meetings have included discussion of China's Most Favoured Nation trade status with the United States, Beijing's accession to the World Trade Organisation, human rights, Hong Kong and Taiwan -- all vital issues in troubled cross-Pacific relations.
"As the saying has it, seeing is believing...increasing mutual exchanges has led to better understanding of each other," Xinhua said.

Sino-U.S. relations chilled last year when Beijing carried out war games near Taiwan and Washington sent two aircraft carrier battlegroups to the area. But both sides say ties have warmed dramatically in recent months.

U.S. President Bill Clinton met President Jiang at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Manila last November and the two agreed on an exchange of presidential visits, the first since early 1989.
New U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is scheduled to visit China in late February, and Vice President Al Gore is to come in late March.
